slides.title: Refresh tokens
slides.subtitle: Keep a user signed in with a rotating token that never leaves the host
slides.notes: A sign-in returns a refresh token, which earlier drafts called the Account Token. This example shows how the agent uses it to get new access tokens, how it rotates, and how it ends. It runs the real RefreshTokenClient against Manzanita Outfitters, with real keys over HTTP in one process.

slides.title: Why refresh tokens
slides.statement: Access tokens are **short-lived**. The refresh token gets a **new one**, without asking the user.
slides.notes: Access tokens expire quickly on purpose. The refresh token is used only at the company's token and revocation endpoints. It is not tied to a Session: any of the User's Sessions can use the access tokens it gets.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB C["RefreshTokenClient"] -- "hold the reference" --> L["pap.refreshTokenLock"] C -- "read, replace" --> S[("pap.tokenStore
holds the refresh token")] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB T["Token endpoint
rotates the token"] R["Revocation endpoint
ends the token"] end HOST -- "grant, client assertion" --> CO HOST -. "status and scopes only" .-> M
slides.caption: The refresh token stays in the host's store; the model learns a status and scope names.
slides.notes: Start inside the host. The RefreshTokenClient holds a lock on the token reference, then reads the refresh token from the Reactor token store and later replaces it there. Only the grant, with a client assertion, crosses to the company, whose token endpoint rotates the token and whose revocation endpoint ends it. Off to the side, the model: it receives only the status and the scope names.

slides.title: A refresh

items.title: Rotate
items.detail: A new access token and a rotated refresh token

items.title: Replace
items.detail: The new token in the store, before unlocking

slides.notes: The client holds the lock, reads the token, and sends a refresh token grant with a client assertion. The grant names no Session. The company returns a new access token and rotates the refresh token. The new one replaces the old in the store before the lock is released and before the call returns.

slides.title: Two refreshes at once
slides.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Refresh A
  participant B as Refresh B
  participant L as Lock
  participant C as Company
  A->>L: Hold the reference
  B->>L: Hold the reference
  A->>C: Grant with token 1
  C-->>A: Access token, token 2
  A->>L: Store token 2, release
  B->>C: Grant with token 2
  C-->>B: Access token, token 3
slides.notes: Two refreshes ask for the same token reference. Refresh A gets the lock first, so B waits for it. Both succeed. A presents token 1, the company rotates it to token 2, and A stores token 2 before releasing the lock. Only then does B go, presenting token 2 rather than the token the company already revoked. Without the lock, both would present token 1 and the second would fail.

slides.title: What the company can answer
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR R["Refresh"] --> Q{"Company answers"} Q -- "rotated" --> S["signed_in
new token stored"] Q -- "invalid_scope" --> C["re_consent_required
ask the user"] Q -- "invalid_grant" --> D["signed_out
token deleted"] V["Revoke"] -- "200" --> X["Sessions go on signed out
token deleted"]
slides.caption: Wider scopes are a decision for the user, never a retry; expiry and revocation delete the token.
slides.notes: Follow a refresh to the company's answer. Usually the token is rotated, the new one is stored, and the result is signed_in; narrower scopes take this path too. Wider scopes come back as invalid_scope, which the SDK reports as re-consent required: a decision for the user, never a retry. Ninety-one days later in the example, the refresh token has expired: the company answers invalid_grant, the SDK deletes the stored copy, and the result is signed_out. Below, revocation under RFC 7009: once the company answers 200 the stored copy is deleted, an access token still in hand is invalid_token, and the Session goes on signed out by sending no token. Sign-out revokes every refresh token held for the account.

slides.title: What stays where
slides.notes: The model learns the status, whether the token rotated, and which scopes it has. Every credential stays in Reactor stores, behind opaque references.

slides.title: In TypeScript
slides.statement: `new RefreshTokenClient({ reactor, fetch })`, with `refresh(reference, { context, scopes })`, `revoke()` and `signOut()`.
slides.notes: TypeScript has the same client, and the lock is contributed at the RefreshTokenLocks contribution point. A token for one MCP server is a refresh with resource set to the server's URL: tokenForMcp in TypeScript, token_for_mcp in Python.
